findings.problem: validate_url_ssrf runs on every InstanceConfig.url when the config loads. Before this change, a hand-edited triggarr.toml with a schemeless URL such as `url = "radarr:7878"` or `url = "192.168.1.10:7878"` still loaded: `url: str` had no format check, and an enabled instance with that URL only produced per-cycle httpx errors, which engine/scheduler already catch. Now validate_arr_url_config returns (False, 'URL scheme must be http or https'), Pydantic raises ValidationError, and ensure_config (triggarr/config.py:345-373) deliberately lets ValidationError propagate uncaught. The same happens for a disabled instance, which never makes HTTP calls. The docstring says rejecting truly unsafe URLs is intended, but schemeless or malformed URLs on disabled instances are a much wider net than metadata or link-local addresses, and the failure mode is a traceback rather than an actionable message. pending: confirm whether schemeless or hand-edited URLs exist in real deployments or v2.2-migrated configs. findings.problem: The new field_validator wires `validate_arr_url_config` (triggarr/web/validation.py:111) into `InstanceConfig.url`, applied unconditionally at model-construction time (including on load from triggarr.toml at startup). This variant deliberately permits loopback IP literals (127.0.0.1, ::1) and the `localhost` DNS name, whereas the stricter `validate_arr_url` used by the settings-page POST handler (triggarr/web/routes.py:561) blocks loopback and runs before `SettingsModel(**new_config)` is constructed. Net effect versus the pre-diff state is a tightening (previously there was zero SSRF check at the model layer for TOML-loaded config), but the specific choice to allow loopback is a real, if intentional, SSRF-surface change: any future code path that constructs `InstanceConfig` from an untrusted or semi-trusted source (not just the already-stricter web form) would now be permitted to point at the local host's other listening ports.
findings.title: New config-load SSRF validator permits loopback URLs the web form rejects
findings.why_it_matters: If any future caller builds InstanceConfig from a less-trusted source than the current TOML-file/authenticated-settings-form paths, the relaxed loopback allowance becomes a usable SSRF primitive against services bound to 127.0.0.1 on the host. Currently this is mitigated because the only web-facing path (routes.py:561) applies the stricter `validate_arr_url` first and rejects loopback before the model is ever constructed, so the relaxed check is reached only for direct TOML edits (a trusted, homelab-admin path) as documented.

agent_notes: No import cycle today: triggarr/web/__init__.py is empty and triggarr/web/validation.py imports only stdlib (ipaddress, re, urllib.parse), so models.config -> web.validation does not load anything that imports models back. The risk is in future edits, not current behavior.

There are now two SSRF policies on purpose: strict validate_arr_url in the settings POST handler (web/routes.py:561) and the relaxed validate_arr_url_config at model construction (models/config.py:106). The docstring presents this as deliberate (D-01/D-02, allowing loopback for same-host *arr installs), so it is not flagged. If the settings POST builds InstanceConfig, both validators run, the strict one wins at the UI boundary, and the relaxed one governs TOML loaded at startup. Reviewers should confirm this split is the intended product behavior: a localhost URL typed in the UI is rejected, but the same URL in the TOML file is accepted.

Consistent with existing pattern: the new validator follows the same @field_validator('url') + @classmethod + raise ValueError(msg) shape as the existing reject_apikey_in_url validator in the same class (config.py lines 64-89). Pydantic runs the two url validators in definition order, so the apikey check runs before the SSRF check.

Blast radius note for impact/bugs lanes: because the validator runs unconditionally, including for disabled instances, an existing user TOML with a metadata/link-local/non-http URL on a disabled instance will now fail Settings construction at startup. The docstring says this hardening is intended, so it is not an architecture finding, but it is an upgrade-compatibility issue worth surfacing.

Unlike reject_apikey_in_url, the new validator does not short-circuit on an empty string (url defaults to ''). Whether validate_arr_url_config('') returns ok determines whether default/unconfigured instances still construct. Not verified here; pending check in tests/test_validation.py / tests/test_config.py.

agent_notes: Change class: this tightens a control. It adds SSRF validation on InstanceConfig.url at model construction. On the SSRF axis it is presumptively safe. I found no bypass in the diff's own lines. Any DNS-hostname bypass (for example a name that resolves to 169.254.169.254) lives in the unchanged helper validate_arr_url_config in triggarr/web/validation.py, which documents it as an accepted residual risk.

Blast radius: InstanceConfig is imported by about 19 production modules (clients, scheduler, engine, routes, startup, state, db) and about 20 test modules. Every construction path now runs the validator: TOML load at startup (triggarr/startup.py:192 -> triggarr/config.py ensure_config), the settings POST (triggarr/web/routes.py:597 SettingsModel(**new_config), where ValidationError is caught and redirects), add-instance (routes.py:790, default url '' passes), and the test-connection path (routes.py:756, ValidationError is caught).

Startup behaviour: ensure_config intentionally does not catch pydantic.ValidationError. A config value that was accepted before and is now rejected becomes a hard crash with a traceback at boot, not a logged warning. Because the validator runs regardless of enabled, a single stale disabled instance blocks all instances. The diff's docstring says this is intended. The concern is how the failure looks to users (no friendly message), not the decision itself.

Pre-existing inconsistency, not introduced here: the web form still uses the strict validate_arr_url (routes.py ~561), which rejects 127.0.0.1/::1 literals, while config load now explicitly accepts them as legitimate. A user with url=http://127.0.0.1:7878 in TOML who edits any setting in the UI and resubmits that instance gets the whole save silently refused (303 redirect, warning log only). 'localhost' as a name passes both validators.

Performance: negligible. The function-local import is cached in sys.modules after the first call, and the validation is one urlparse plus ipaddress parse per instance at config load and save. There is no request-path cost.
Schema/migration: no DB or TOML schema change. Existing on-disk configs are re-validated with stricter rules on the next boot, which is the main upgrade risk (impact-1).
Circular import check: triggarr/web/validation.py imports only stdlib, so the lazy import from models/config.py does not create a cycle. A top-level import would also be safe.
Verification: uv run pytest tests/ -x -q gives 982 passed.
Verdict: shippable. Consider a friendly ValidationError handler in ensure_config and a release note about 0.0.0.0 and scheme-less URLs before tagging.

Before this change these TOML values loaded fine. On Linux, http://0.0.0.0:<port> in fact connects to the local host. Users often copy 0.0.0.0 from the *arr 'Bind Address' setting, so a same-host deployment that works today can hit this. After upgrade, ensure_config() -> load_settings() raises pydantic.ValidationError. ensure_config (triggarr/config.py:340-345) deliberately lets ValidationError through uncaught, so the daemon exits with a traceback at triggarr/startup.py:192. Under Docker restart policies the container then restarts in a loop. There is no friendly log line and no hint to fix the URL. One bad instance, even a disabled one, takes down every configured Radarr/Sonarr/Lidarr instance. The docstring says rejecting unsafe disabled instances is intended (D-01/D-02). The only open question is whether 0.0.0.0 is a supported value or out of contract. pending: confirm whether 0.0.0.0 or a scheme-less disabled-instance URL appears in real user configs or docs.
